## Primary data

**1. U.S. Department of Education, College Scorecard**
Most Recent Cohorts institution file and historical archive (1996-97 to
2025-26), June 2026 release. Washington, DC: U.S. Department of Education,
Office of Planning, Evaluation and Policy Development.
[collegescorecard.ed.gov](https://collegescorecard.ed.gov/) ·
[data documentation](https://collegescorecard.ed.gov/data/)

Provides institution-level cost, aid, enrollment, completion, debt, and
post-enrollment earnings data for nearly every degree-granting institution in
the United States. Used for the cross-sectional analysis (sticker price, net
price by income bracket, debt, earnings, and the earnings regression) and,
via the historical archive, the 25-year tuition trend.

**2. Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (FRED) / U.S. Bureau of Labor
Statistics**
Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers: All Items in U.S. City Average
(CPIAUCSL), seasonally adjusted, monthly.
[fred.stlouisfed.org/series/CPIAUCSL](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/CPIAUCSL)

Used to convert nominal dollar figures across different years into constant
2025 dollars, so tuition and cost figures from different academic years can
be compared on an inflation-adjusted basis.

**3. Chetty, Raj, John N. Friedman, Emmanuel Saez, Nicholas Turner, and Danny
Yagan. "Mobility Report Cards: The Role of Colleges in Intergenerational
Mobility."** NBER Working Paper No. 23618, National Bureau of Economic
Research, 2017 (Opportunity Insights).
[opportunityinsights.org/paper/mrc](https://opportunityinsights.org/paper/mrc/) ·
[NBER working paper](https://www.nber.org/papers/w23618)

An independent analysis, built on de-identified federal tax and enrollment
records rather than the Scorecard's institution-reported averages, of the
family-income distribution and post-college outcomes of students at
"Ivy-Plus" colleges — a group that includes Stanford. Cited here for
context on *who* enrolls at elite private universities, complementing this
project's focus on what those students pay and earn. Independently
corroborates the shape of this project's finding that aid is steeply
need-based while access still skews toward higher-income families.

## How these sources relate to this project's data pipeline

`scripts/download.py` fetches sources 1 and 2 programmatically; both are
public and machine-readable. Source 3 is a published research paper cited
for narrative and methodological context rather than pulled into the
pipeline — its underlying microdata (IRS and NSLDS records linked at the
individual level) is not publicly downloadable and is not part of this
project's analysis universe.

Full data-cleaning and modeling detail: [Methods](methods.qmd).
